entry.title: Roadmap
entry.content:
Roadmap

No package in this repository has had a stable release yet, and the language itself is still settling — see the repository README for where the language grammar stands. This page is about something narrower: which implementations of tramaj exist, and which are wanted next.

Where things stand today

Six independent implementations target the same grammar and are checked against a shared, language-neutral conformance corpus — template/context/expected-output triples that all must reproduce byte-for-byte, per case, in both concrete and symbolic evaluation modes. That’s a deliberately strong bar: a case belongs in the corpus only if independently written implementations can run it identically.

ImplementationLanguageStatus
tramajPureScriptreference implementation, checked against the corpus; tramaj-halogen folds to Halogen, tramaj-cli is its CLI
tramaj-hsHaskellindependent port, checked against the same corpus
tramaj-rsRustindependent port, checked against the same corpus; tramaj-cli-rs is its CLI
tramaj-jsJavaScript / TypeScriptindependent port, checked against the same corpus; tramaj-react folds to React
tramaj-pyPythonindependent port on the standard library alone, checked against the same corpus; python -m tramaj is its CLI
tramaj-goGoindependent port on the standard library alone, checked against the same corpus; tramaj-go is its CLI

tramaj-purs and tramaj-halogen are on the PureScript registry (0.4.1), tramaj-hs on Hackage (0.4.0.0), tramaj-rs and tramaj-cli-rs on crates.io (0.2.0), and tramaj-py on PyPI as tramaj (0.2.0), each with language v5. tramaj-js, tramaj-react, tramaj-go and tramaj-cli are in no package registry yet, and are used as source or git dependencies. Each has its own changelog page and Atom feed. See Integrating tramaj for what’s actually usable from each right now, including the fold each one does or doesn’t ship.

The native-implementation wish list is done

Earlier versions of this page asked for native JavaScript, Python and Rust implementations, so that hosts in those ecosystems would get what PureScript and Haskell hosts already had: an in-process parser and evaluator, with no subprocess and no JSON round-trip just to get a Node. All three exist now — tramaj-js, tramaj-py and tramaj-rs — and each passes the full corpus in both modes, v3 and v4 extensions included. A Go port, tramaj-go, has since joined them on the same terms.

Language v5, in all six: two number types, arithmetic, sorting and number formatting

Numbers are now an integer and a float, two types, and a template can compute with ten named arithmetic builtins, round among them. It can also sort a list with sort-by and sort-by-descending, and write a number with format-number. Together these are language v5, announced here. The specification and the corpus fixtures are written, and all six implementations have all of it:

ImplementationLanguage v5Released in
tramaj (PureScript), tramaj-halogen, tramaj-cli, playgroundyestramaj-purs and tramaj-halogen 0.4.1 (PureScript registry)
tramaj-hsyes0.4.0.0 (Hackage)
tramaj-js, tramaj-reactyeson main; not on npm yet
tramaj-rs, tramaj-cli-rsyes0.2.0 (crates.io)
tramaj-goyeson main, no tagged version
tramaj-pyyes0.2.0 (PyPI, as tramaj)

The corpus cases for these carry a "profiles" field, and an implementation skips the cases that list a name it does not provide. All six provide every name but one: the integer range, 53 bits in PureScript and TypeScript and 64 bits in the other four, so each skips the few cases written for the other range. The number split and the arithmetic profile are no longer skippable: a case that lists "int-float" or "arithmetic" fails in an implementation that does not provide it. The split changes existing output: Migrating to integers and floats lists how.

?shape is an accepted design without normative text, and no implementation has it. See Two designs accepted.

Desired next: folds, and npm

  • Folds. Only PureScript (tramaj-halogen) and JavaScript (tramaj-react) ship a fold to a rendering target. A DOM fold for JS, a fold to a common Python templating output, and a fold for at least one Haskell or Rust UI or markup library are the obvious next pieces.
  • npm packages. crates.io, PyPI, Hackage and the PureScript registry have a v5 release; npm has only a 0.0.0-stage placeholder, and a release of tramaj-js and tramaj-react is wanted there. Releases happen when there are major changes, and each package’s version tracks the language version it implements in its major digit.

This is a wish list, not a schedule: there’s no committed timeline or assigned owner for any of it.

What “done” looks like for a new implementation

tramaj-hs, tramaj-rs, tramaj-js, tramaj-py and tramaj-go are the templates to follow, since they were added after the language had settled on a normative spec and output format (tramaj-py is the smallest: one module per concern, standard library only). A new implementation is considered on par with the existing ones once it:

  • implements the grammar and evaluation rules in reference.md, including the static restrictions that make imports, action keys, and ctx(...) paths analyzable without evaluation (see Properties);
  • encodes and decodes the Node AST exactly per node-json.md, including the round-trip guarantee (decode(encode(n)) == n);
  • passes every case in the conformance corpus, in both concrete and symbolic mode, byte-for-byte against expected.json;
  • optionally, but ideally: a fold analogous to tramaj-halogen’s foldToHalogen for at least one popular rendering target in that ecosystem (e.g. a DOM fold for JS, a common Python templating output for Python).

The v3 (?/!, v3-symbols.md) and v4 (%, v4-types.md) extensions are both shipped and part of the same conformance bar — a new implementation isn’t considered complete while targeting only the v2 core.

Contributing an implementation

If you’re taking on one of these, the corpus is the fastest way to find out what you got wrong: it’s meant to be run against a from-scratch implementation just as it’s run against the six that exist, and a case that byte-for-byte matches all of them today is a strong signal your evaluation semantics agree with theirs. Open an issue on the repository before investing heavily in one — coordinating on which language is being worked on avoids duplicate effort.
entry.summary: Six implementations exist today: PureScript, Haskell, Rust, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python and Go, all held to one conformance corpus. All six carry the whole of language v5 (integers and floats as two types, arithmetic, sorting and number formatting) and run the whole corpus. Wanted next: npm packages and folds.

entry.title: tramaj v5: numbers that compute, in all six implementations
entry.content:
tramaj v5: numbers that compute, in all six implementations

tramaj has gone through four iterations so far: v1 (the original block/template split), v2 (expression-oriented documents, static analyses and the Node JSON format), v3 (symbols and constraints) and v4 (types). This is the fifth. It changes what a number is, and lets a template do something with one:

  • Two number types. An integer and a float, with no implicit conversion between them.
  • Arithmetic. Ten named builtins, round among them, in an optional profile that a host turns on.
  • Sorting. sort-by and sort-by-descending order a list by a key function.
  • Number formatting. format-number writes a number with a fixed number of decimals and a group separator, rounded the same way everywhere.

And the part that makes it a version rather than a design: all six implementations have all of it, and run the same corpus.

@rows=sort-by-descending($ctx.rows, (r) => $r.spend)
@total=sum(map($rows, (r) => $r.spend))
.table(
  map($rows, (r) => .tr(.td($r.name), .td(format-number($r.spend, 2, ","))))
  , .tr(.td("total"), .td(format-number($total, 2, ","))))

What changed since v4

Numbers. A JSON number in the context is typed by its text: 3 is an integer, 3.0 and 3e0 are floats. A template literal follows the same rule. Integers are exact over a guaranteed range; an integer outside it is refused instead of being rounded. Comparisons do not mix the two types, and real(…), floor(…) and round(…) convert when the template asks.

Arithmetic. Until v4 the reference said a template “compares and selects, it does not compute”. That is reversed, narrowly: the grammar has no infix operators, and arithmetic is ten named builtins (sum, product, negate, round, …) in a profile the host enables. A host that does not enable it can refuse such a program up front, from its static analysis, without evaluating it. The design and the alternatives that were rejected are in Two designs accepted.

Sorting and formatting. sort-by(list, fn) and sort-by-descending(list, fn) order a list by the key fn gives each element, and are stable. format-number(x, decimals, group) writes 1234567.891 as "1,234,567.89". Both are part of the core language and need no profile. The rounding rule of format-number is normative, because the native formatters of the six host languages disagree on ties and on negative zero: each implementation writes the rule by hand rather than calling its own formatter.

All of this is specified in reference.md §3, §11 and §13, and recorded, with the alternatives, in specs/decisions.md sections 18 and 20.

Breaking changes

The arithmetic profile is an addition: a template that does not use it is unaffected. The number split is not optional, and it changes the output of some existing templates and hosts:

whatv4v5
str of a whole-valued floatstr(1.0) is 1str(1.0) is 1.0
eq across the two typeseq(1, 1.0) is truefalse
lt, lte, gt, gte across the two typesgt(1.5, 0) is truea TypeMismatch
a JSON number in the contexta double, whatever its text3 is an integer, 3.0 and 3e0 are floats
an integer outside the rangerounded to the nearest doublerefused: a parse error as a literal, a TypeMismatch in the context
the object key "$term"an ordinary keyreserved, like "$sym" and "$type"
the type primitive number (v4 types)a primitivegone: int and float replace it

Migrating to integers and floats takes each row in turn: who it affects, how to find the templates it affects, and what to change.

Every implementation runs the whole corpus

The conformance corpus holds 646 cases: a template, a context and the expected output, compared byte for byte, in both concrete and symbolic mode. Until now an implementation could skip a case that needed a profile it did not provide, and while the ports caught up, some did. That is over: "int-float" and "arithmetic" are now required of every runner, and a case that lists one fails, rather than being skipped, in an implementation without it.

The only cases any implementation still skips are the ones written for the other integer range. PureScript and TypeScript have the guaranteed 53-bit range, because their host number is a double; the other four have the 64-bit range. Each skips the few cases that pin down the other range’s edges.

implementationinteger rangecorpus
tramaj (PureScript)53-bitpasses; skips only the 64-bit range cases
tramaj-hs (Haskell)64-bitpasses; skips only the 53-bit range cases
tramaj-rs (Rust)64-bitpasses; skips only the 53-bit range cases
tramaj-js (TypeScript)53-bitpasses; skips only the 64-bit range cases
tramaj-go (Go)64-bitpasses; skips only the 53-bit range cases
tramaj-py (Python)64-bitpasses; skips only the 53-bit range cases

Packages

Where to get v5 today:

packagelanguagewhere
tramaj-purs, tramaj-halogenPureScriptPureScript registry, 0.4.1
tramaj-cliPureScriptfrom the repository
tramaj-hsHaskellHackage, 0.4.0.0
tramaj-rs, tramaj-cli-rsRustcrates.io, 0.2.0
tramaj (tramaj-py)PythonPyPI, 0.2.0
@lucasdicioccio/tramaj-js, @lucasdicioccio/tramaj-reactTypeScriptfrom the repository; npm has only a placeholder so far
tramaj-goGofrom the repository, as github.com/lucasdicioccio/tramaj/tramaj-go, at a commit on main

Each package has its own changelog page and Atom feed. Integrating tramaj says how to depend on each one.

What’s next

v5 is a fifth iteration, not a stable release: the language can still change. The roadmap lists what is wanted next: the npm packages and folds to more rendering targets. Beyond v5, ?shape is an accepted design for allocating a structure of symbols in one form; no implementation has it yet.
entry.summary: The fifth iteration of the language is out. Numbers are an integer and a float, a template can compute, sort a list and format a number, and all six implementations run the whole conformance corpus. Some existing output changes.

entry.title: Two designs accepted: arithmetic, and shapes of symbols
entry.content:
Two designs accepted: arithmetic, and shapes of symbols

Two language designs were accepted this week. This page says what each one is and how far along it is. The short version:

designacceptedspecifiedimplemented
arithmetic, and integers and floats as two types2026-10-06yes, in the referenceall six implementations, with the command-line tools, the Halogen fold and the playground, on main, not released
?shape, a form that allocates a structure of symbols2026-10-08design onlyno

Both are recorded in specs/decisions.md, sections 18 and 19, with the alternatives that were rejected and why.

Arithmetic

Until now the reference said a template “compares and selects, it does not compute”. Every derived number was the host’s job. That works when the host and the template author are the same party. It fails when a template is handed counters by a host it does not control: it cannot show a subtotal or a share in percent unless someone upstream precomputes each one and stores it next to the raw numbers.

So the position is reversed, narrowly. The grammar does not change. There are no infix operators. Arithmetic is nine named builtins:

builtinoperandsresult
sum(…), product(…)all integers or all floatsthe sum, the product
negate(x)an integer or a float-x, of the same type
quotient(a, b), inverse(x)floatsfloat division
floor-quotient(a, b), modulo(a, b)integersinteger division and its remainder
floor(x)eitherthe largest integer not above x
real(x)eitherthe float nearest to x
@subtotal = sum($ctx.compute, $ctx.storage, negate($ctx.credit))
@share    = branch(0, gt($ctx.total, 0),
                   floor-quotient(product(100, $ctx.used), $ctx.total))
@total    = sum(0.0, map($ctx.lines,
                         (l) => product(real($l.qty), real($l.price))))

Integers and floats are two types

A counter must add exactly and a ratio must not, so the single number type splits in two. A literal with neither a fraction nor an exponent is an integer (1, -7); one with either is a float (1.0, 1e5). A JSON number in the context is read by the same rule.

Nothing converts between the two unless the program says so. sum(1, 2.5) is an error, eq(1, 1.0) is false, and gt(1.5, 0) is written gt(1.5, 0.0). real and floor are the two conversions, and each accepts both types, so a template that does not know which one its host sends normalizes with real($x).

This changes existing output in one case. A float keeps its type when it is written, so a whole-valued float renders with a fraction: str(1.0) is 1.0 where it was 1. An integer renders as before.

Over a symbol, arithmetic builds a term

In symbolic mode a number may not be known yet. sum(1, $s, 2) with a symbol $s does not fail and does not guess. It evaluates to a term, the computation handed to the host undone:

{"$term": "sum", "arguments": [1, {"$sym": "#0:\"s\"", "path": []}, 2]}

The operands are kept exactly as written, with nothing folded. That buys one law: a host that substitutes numbers for the symbols and evaluates the term by the reference’s rules gets what the template would have produced had those numbers been in the context. Tramaj still solves nothing.

Where it stands

The normative text is in the language reference and the symbols reference, and the conformance corpus has the fixtures. All six implementations (PureScript, Haskell, TypeScript, Rust, Go and Python) have the number split and the builtins on main, and so do the command-line tools (tramaj-cli --arithmetic), the Halogen fold and the playground. They are not in a release. A tenth builtin, round, was added to the nine above by the third design, below.

The split changes what some existing templates produce, beyond the str case above: see Migrating to integers and floats.

?shape: a structure of symbols in one form

In symbolic mode a template allocates a solver variable with ?(key). One variable at a time is fine. A structure of them is not: every variable is its own form, with a key composed by hand.

@cluster = {
  lb:         ?(["cluster", "lb"]),
  placements: map($ctx.vms, (vm) => {
    vm:   $vm.name,
    host: ?(["cluster", "host", $vm.name]),
    zone: ?(["cluster", "zone", $vm.name])
  })
}

The accepted design adds a second allocation form. ?shape(key, shape) takes the key once, and the shape says where the symbols go with a named marker, ~name:

@cluster = ?shape("cluster", {
  ~lb,
  placements: map($ctx.vms, (vm) => {vm: $vm.name, ~host($vm.name), ~zone($vm.name)})
})

This is “traverse” in the functional-programming sense: walk a structure, run an effect at each position, get the same structure back. The effect is allocation. The number of placements is whatever the caller’s vms holds.

The rules are few:

  • A marker is explicit and named. ~lb is a symbol; nothing else in the shape is. {~lb} is short for {lb: ~lb}.
  • A marker may be written anywhere in the shape: a field, an array element, a call’s argument, the body of a map.
  • Under a lambda a marker carries its own key, ~host($vm.name), which says which iteration it belongs to. A bare marker there is a parse error, so one variable is never shared across iterations by accident.
  • Identity is what the author wrote. The symbols above are #0:["cluster","lb"], #0:["cluster","host","a"] and so on: the form’s key, the marker’s name and the marker’s key. No position and no index is involved, so reordering the vms keeps every variable’s identity.
  • Mistakes are parse errors: the same marker name twice in one form, or a shape with no marker at all.

It is a pure rewriting onto ?(key). The form above means exactly what the hand-written version means, so the core language, the output envelope and every host decoder stay as they are.

Where it stands

This one is a design only. The normative text is not written and no implementation has it. PureScript and Haskell come first, as for arithmetic. One thing it does not cover is a caller that supplies a count rather than a list: that needs a range, which is a separate question.

Also accepted: sorting and number formatting

A third design was accepted on the same day, in section 20 of the same file: sort-by(list, fn) and sort-by-descending(list, fn), which take a key function as map does, and format-number(x, decimals, group), which turns 1234567.891 into 1,234,567.89 by one rounding rule every implementation must agree on, with round as a tenth arithmetic builtin. Its normative text is now in the language reference, marked [§20], and all six implementations have it on main, in no release yet.
entry.summary: A template can now compute with numbers, and will soon declare a whole structure of solver variables in one form. Both designs are written down and accepted; neither is in a release yet.
